A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright. Slavish reproduction of public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). Original additions such as a new score, colorization, or new titles can be protected. The Internet Archive item includes a colourised version, and any such colorization can carry its own protection. Use archival prints rather than ripping a commercial disc, because ripping a copy-protected disc can implicate 17 U.S.C. § 1201.

editorial:
Plan 9 from Outer Space is a science-fiction horror film that Ed Wood produced, wrote, directed and edited for Reynolds Pictures, Inc. Wikipedia reports that it was shot in black and white in November 1956 at Quality Studios in Los Angeles on a $60,000 budget. It previewed at the Carlton Theatre in Los Angeles on March 15, 1957, and was released in July 1958. It is known as an alleged 'worst film ever made'. The Public Domain Review catalogs it under 1959 and lists the underlying work as 'PD U.S.', but cites no registration or renewal search and marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear'.

The rights trap is that nobody has shown the status with a primary record. We could not run a Copyright Office registration or renewal search, so the print is undetermined. The soundtrack is also a compilation: Gordon Zahler assembled it from stock recordings in Lee Zahler's mood-music library, and those tracks may have their own histories. The Internet Archive item also carries a colourised version, which can be protected on its own. Treat the film as unverified until a registration and renewal search is done, and get advice before reusing footage commercially.
faq: Can I use Plan 9 from Outer Space footage in my own film or video?

Not safely, as far as we can verify. The Public Domain Review lists the film as 'PD U.S.', but cites no registration or renewal search, and we could not run one. The status is undetermined until a Copyright Office search is done. Get advice before reusing footage commercially.
Does an Internet Archive copy or a Creative Commons label mean I can reuse it?

No. A hosting label on an uploaded copy does not decide the film's copyright status. The Public Domain Review marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear', and added material such as the colourised version or a new score can be protected on its own.
